title: Termites: They Bore But They Aren't Boring
summary: Josh and Chuck explore termites, taking a listener suggestion from Aaron Mullins. They cover termite biology and social structure (castes of king and queen, reproductives, soldiers, workers), pheromone population control, cellulose digestion with gut microorganisms, fungus-farming termites, nest types (subterranean, mound-builders, wood-dwelling primitives), shelter tubes, mound climate control and biomimicry, the nuptial swarm and founding of new colonies, lifespans, termites' ecological role, and how to prevent, detect, and treat infestations. The episode closes with listener mail about a fourth-grade bird incident and a couple of anti-jokes.

segments.title: Listener suggestion and opening banter
segments.summary: Josh introduces the episode as a suggestion from listener Aaron Mullins and banter about termites being fascinating; Chuck and Josh tease the topic.

segments.title: Termite anatomy, range, and sociality
segments.summary: Termites are social insects found mostly in tropical areas but also temperate climates, about fifty million years old with nearly three thousand species, and more closely related to cockroaches than ants. Colonies have a caste structure.

segments.title: Reproductives, eyes, and pheromones
segments.summary: The king and queen are the only fully mature, dark-colored members and are the primary reproducers, with secondary and tertiary reproductives as backup. Eyes are mostly limited to reproductives; the blind members navigate by scent and moisture trails. Pheromones regulate colony population and caste development.

segments.title: Soldier termites
segments.summary: Soldiers defend the nest against other termites and ants, with large mandibles. Some have blue sacs of toxic fluid they burst as a suicidal defense, and some soldiers shoot feces at enemies. Their regurgitated spittle can be sticky or toxic.

segments.title: Worker termites and cellulose digestion
segments.summary: Workers are blind and do most labor, including eating wood, digging tunnels, gathering food, and feeding other castes. Termites cannot digest cellulose on their own; gut protozoans and bacteria break it down.

segments.title: Primitive vs higher termites and development
segments.summary: Termites are classified as primitive (wood-nesting) or higher (mound-builders, about three quarters of species). Development goes through egg, larva, molts, and nymph stages; any nymph can become any caste, and reverse molting is possible.

segments.title: Swarming, nuptial flight, and founding new colonies
segments.summary: When colonies grow large, winged reproductives swarm on a warm humid day in a nuptial flight. Mates pair, shed wings, and dig a chamber sealed with poop and saliva. The new queen lays eggs; a colony takes two to four years to mature. Colonies swarm at the same time to keep gene pools diverse. Queens can live around twenty to twenty-five years, workers two to five years.

segments.title: Nests, mounds, and subterranean termites
segments.summary: Subterranean nests are underground networks with galleries, connected to food sources, and shift to warmer or shaded areas. Shelter tubes cross obstacles. Mounds of soil, excrement, and saliva are climate-controlled and durable; the Eastgate Centre in Harare uses termite-inspired ventilation. Some termites farm fungus that breaks down cellulose.

segments.title: Termites' ecological role and frass
segments.summary: Termites are eaten by many animals and break down dead wood and animal dung, playing a vital ecological role. Their feces, frass, is rich in magnesium and enriches soil.

segments.title: Termite prevention, detection, and extermination
segments.summary: Prevention includes keeping wood off the ground, moisture barriers, and pre-construction soil treatment. Signs include swarms, shelter tubes, hollow-sounding wood, and tiny wings; termites differ from ants in waist, wings, and antennae. Professional options include baits, repellents, and soil treatments, with inspections before buying a house.
